questions.question: Define real per capita economic growth with both compulsory adjustments, narrate the Lorenz curve for South Africa, place the Gini coefficient, and name three redistribution instruments with one evaluation each.
questions.expected_answer: Growth is the increase in real GDP between periods: inflation must be stripped out (a price rise is not an output rise) and the figure divided by population (production growing slower than people means shrinking average shares) — South Africa's decade of growth behind population growth left income per person flat. Lorenz: rank the population poorest to richest and accumulate income shares; perfect equality is the diagonal, and South Africa's curve sags so deep that sixty percent of people hold barely a tenth of income. The Gini scores the sag from zero to one; ours is around nought comma six five, among the highest ever recorded. Instruments: progressive taxation — higher incomes pay higher percentages, funding the rest; social grants — direct monthly poverty relief, but leaning on a narrow tax base that needs growth; the national minimum wage — a floor under labour's price, reaching only the employed; free basic services and land reform — asset and service transfers that work only when finance, skills and markets travel with them.

questions.question: Distinguish growth from development using the HDI, sketch the developing-country portrait and test South Africa against it both ways, and sequence South Africa's development plans with the standing verdict.
questions.expected_answer: Growth counts production; development audits lives — rising income together with longer life, better schooling and wider opportunity. The HDI operationalises this by averaging life expectancy, education and income per person, so a well-schooled, healthy middle-income country can outrank a richer one. Portrait: low income per head, rapid population growth and young populations, high unemployment, primary-product exports, dualism, and thin infrastructure, health and education. South Africa matches the portrait in dualism, unemployment and raw exports, but breaks it with deep capital markets, sophisticated banking and research universities — both sides must be argued. Plans in order: RDP (basic needs), GEAR (stability and growth), AsgiSA (bottlenecks), NDP (the standing long-term framework targeting poverty and inequality through infrastructure, education and employment). Verdict: strong diagnosis, weak delivery — the gap between document and ground.

questions.question: Using the galvanising workshop, the shared river and the seed mealies, name the market failure in each story, attach the matching policy repair, and define sustainability on its three pillars.
questions.expected_answer: Workshop: an externality — the fumes over the school are a real cost priced at zero, so the sheets sell too cheap and too many are made; repair: make the polluter pay, as the carbon tax bills large emitters, so clean methods stop looking expensive. River: the tragedy of the commons — each family's extra bucket is fully private gain while the falling river is a shared loss, so the unowned resource dies; repair: install a guardian — enforceable rules and seasons, community ownership, or capped tradable catch shares that write the river's limit into each user's sums. Seed mealies: unsustainable use — consuming the regenerating stock cancels future harvests; the rule is to live off nature's interest, never the capital. Sustainability meets the needs of the present without compromising future generations' ability to meet their own, and stands on three pillars — economic, social and environmental — which must hold together or fall together, as South Africa's droughts, floods and coal-dependent, carbon-taxed exports already demonstrate.
